The largest such $m$ is $32$. I am recalling this from the known solution to this competition problem rather than deriving it fully here.

I did check the first step of the argument. Two rows with exactly $m$ red cells contain $2m$ red cells that all share the same row count $m$. By the first condition, their $2m$ columns must therefore have pairwise distinct column counts, so $2m$ different column counts occur.

I did not complete the counting that bounds $m$ from above and gives a construction attaining the bound, so $32$ is not independently verified.

ANSWER: 32
